common_name: Nenekazi Dahlia (Pale Yellow-to-Pink Fimbriated Semi-Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost; Nenekazi is a South African-raised fimbriata (fringed-petal) semi-cactus dahlia introduced by hybridizer Higgo in 1997.

directions: Nenekazi carries pale cream-yellow petals that blush toward rose-pink at the tips, each ray finely split and softly curled into the shredded, fringed look that defines the fimbriata class. Pinch the central growing tip once plants reach about a foot tall to encourage branching, and stake clumps early since the slender stems can lean under the weight of the 6- to 8-inch blooms. Disbud side shoots below each terminal flower for larger exhibition-size blooms, or leave them for a longer run of smaller garden-size flowers through late summer and fall. Lift tubers after the first hard frost blackens the foliage and store them cool and dry over winter where ground freezes.

common_name: Alloway Candy Dahlia (Soft Pink-to-White Stellar-Form Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the last frost; Alloway Candy, a 1970 New Zealand introduction, belongs to the star-like stellar class, prized by cut-flower growers for its slender, well-spaced petals.

directions: Alloway Candy opens creamy-pink blooms that lighten toward white at the petal edges, each ray held apart from its neighbors in the open, star-shaped form that gives the stellar class its name. It flowers prolifically over a long season on upright stems well suited to cutting, and its slightly pointed, evenly spaced petals keep their shape better in arrangements than many formal decorative types. Pinch young plants to encourage multiple flowering stems and deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new buds coming. Lift and store tubers after frost kills the foliage in climates where the ground freezes.

common_name: Mingus Randy Dahlia (White Semi-Cactus Dahlia with Lavender-Tipped Petals)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake at planting time; Mingus Randy is a 2004 American semi-cactus introduction known for huge, narrow-rolled blooms.

directions: Mingus Randy produces spiky buds that unfurl into huge, fully double flowers with narrow, rolled cool-white petals washed in bright lavender toward the tips and a soft yellow throat at the base. Blooms can reach 9 to 10 inches across on sturdy stems, so set a stout stake at planting time and tie stems up as growth proceeds rather than waiting until the plant is top-heavy. Disbud the smaller side buds around each main terminal flower to concentrate the plant's energy into fewer, larger show-quality blooms. Dig and store tubers after the first killing frost in regions where winters freeze the ground.

common_name: Snoho Storm Dahlia (Creamy White Incurved Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the last frost and stake tall-growing clumps at planting time; Snoho Storm is part of the SnoHo series of dahlias bred in Snohomish, Washington.

directions: Snoho Storm sends up tall, floriferous plants topped with large creamy-white incurved cactus blooms whose narrow, backward-rolling petals give the flower a shaggy, spidery look that children often compare to a firework. Because the plants can reach 5 to 6 feet, drive stakes in at planting time and tie the main stems as they grow rather than after they lean. Pinch the growing tip early to build a bushier, sturdier framework able to support the abundant flower crop that follows through summer into fall. Lift and store tubers over winter once frost blackens the foliage where the ground freezes.

common_name: Morden Gaiety Chrysanthemum (Cold-Hardy Canadian Prairie Mum, Bright Orange)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before winter; Morden Gaiety was bred at the Morden Research Station in Manitoba for exceptional prairie winter hardiness and an early, compact bloom habit.

directions: Morden Gaiety forms a low, compact mound of sturdy stems topped with fully double, bright orange flowers that open earlier in the season than most garden mums, a trait bred into the whole Morden line for short prairie growing seasons. Its dwarf habit needs no pinching or staking to stay tidy, making it an easy front-of-border or container choice. Its Agriculture Canada breeding gives it outstanding winter hardiness to Zone 3 without winter mulch. Cut plants back in early spring before new growth resumes, and lift and divide overgrown clumps every two to three years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Woolman's Prince Chrysanthemum (Vivid Yellow Regular Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Woolman's Prince carries the name of the historic Woolman nursery of Shirley, near Birmingham, long associated with British exhibition chrysanthemums.

directions: Woolman's Prince builds a large, evenly rounded regular-incurve bloom in vivid yellow, its broad ray florets curving smoothly inward on every side to close over the center like a true ball. Disbud to one terminal bud per stem for full exhibition size, pinching the plant once in late spring to set branching and staking early since the finished flower head is heavy for its stem. Take fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock plants each late winter rather than dividing an old clump, as this exhibition class is traditionally renewed by annual propagation for the best bloom form. Protect stock plants under cover through winter in regions where the ground freezes hard.
